title: One Template, Many Types: A Ring Buffer That Works for Anything

questions.question: Ring<T, Capacity> has two template parameters. What is different about Capacity?
options: It is a non type parameter, a number known at compile time, which is what lets the storage be a plain array inside the object
Nothing: both are types, and Capacity happens to be std::size_t
It is optional, and defaults to whatever the first push needs
It is a runtime argument, passed to the constructor
questions.explanation: Because the capacity is known while the code compiles, the array can be a member rather than a heap allocation. Measured: 1000 pushes into a Ring<double, 64> performed 0 allocations, and sizeof is 528 bytes of which 512 are the doubles.

questions.question: In a ring buffer, why is slot(index) not just index?
options: Positions count from the oldest element, and the oldest moves as the buffer is reused
Because arrays in C++ are one based
To leave room for the bookkeeping at the start of the array
It is the same, and the function exists only for readability
questions.explanation: That one line is the whole idea of a ring buffer. Returning storage_[index] reads the right set of elements in the wrong order once the buffer has wrapped, which is invisible until the buffer fills for the first time.

questions.question: A Ring<double, 4> has had 1 to 7 pushed into it. What does oldest() return?
options: 4, because it is the oldest reading still held, not the first one ever pushed
1, the first thing that was pushed
7, since the oldest slot now holds the newest value
An error, because three readings were discarded
questions.explanation: The ring holds 4 5 6 7. Overwriting the oldest rather than refusing the push is the decision that makes this a history: a sensor does not stop producing readings because your buffer is full.

questions.question: Are Ring<double, 4> and Ring<int, 4> the same class?
options: No: they share a definition and nothing else, so each has its own code and its own statics
Yes, with the element type erased at runtime
Yes, since the capacity is the same
Only if double and int are the same size
questions.explanation: Each instantiation is separate code. Pushing into one leaves the other at size zero, and sizeof(Ring<double, 8>) is 80 against 48 for Ring<double, 4>. It is also why a template in a header costs compile time per type and per translation unit.

questions.question: Calling std::sort on a vector of a type with no operator< gave 113 lines of error on gcc. Adding a static_assert to your own template changed that to 5. What did it do on clang?
options: It went up, to 254 lines from 224, because clang reports the assertion and then instantiates the rest anyway
It went down to about 5 lines as well
It had no effect at all
It became a warning rather than an error
questions.explanation: So the obvious conclusion is half wrong. What a static_assert reliably fixes on both compilers is the first error line, which becomes a sentence you wrote naming your own file, instead of a libstdc++ header 21 instantiation frames deep.

questions.question: Where should the static_assert constraining a template go?
options: In your own template, at the edge of your code, so the first error names your file
As deep as possible, nearest the operation that actually fails
In the caller, before the call
It does not matter: the compiler reports the same thing either way
questions.explanation: Putting it deeper does not help, because deeper is where the problem already was. And write the message as an instruction rather than a complaint: needs numbers, pass int or double tells the reader what to do, which matters because the first line is the one that gets read.
